Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette:
Karim is a 78-year-old roofer of Middle Eastern descent, married for over fifty years. Forty years on roofs had left him with a deep knowledge of materials and a quiet pride in his work—until the day he was tearing off old tar and fiberboard on a school roof, and a plume of chemical fumes from decades-old insulation burned his throat and sent him to the hospital. He spent two weeks in intensive care with solvent poisoning, and though his lungs recovered, something else did not.

In the months that followed, Karim found he could not deliberately call up the details of that morning—the exact order of events, the faces of the workers beside him—but the feeling would arrive without warning. Sometimes he would be sitting in his living room and a wave of pure panic would wash over him, his chest tight, his skin tingling, no image in his mind, only the helplessness. At other times a trigger would bring the memory rushing back with full force. He had come to believe that seeing children was the worst of them, because their voices had been drifting into the schoolyard just before he collapsed. When he now sees a child playing nearby, the sound cuts through him like a blade, and the moment returns—the burning in his throat, the spinning world—unbidden and vivid.

That rush of memory always left him rigid with alarm. For hours afterward his heart hammered at the slightest touch; if his wife laid a hand on his shoulder from behind, he would jump and swat it away before his mind caught up. He could not relax even when he was sure he was safe, and at night he lay awake for hours, replaying the panic without being able to recall the details he wanted. The memory itself became something he dreaded, so he began to avoid the triggers with growing vigilance. He stopped walking past the elementary school. He stopped visiting his son’s family because his grandchildren were there. He even told his wife to change the channel whenever a news story mentioned chemical exposure or industrial accidents. But his constant scanning—his habit of checking every street corner for children, every headline for danger—meant he noticed potential triggers far more often than he used to. His avoidance made the world seem full of threats.

And the threat itself fed back into the triggers. Karim was so seldom at ease, so primed to startle, that any unexpected contact could set him off. When his wife touched his arm in a grocery store aisle, his body reacted before his mind could register who it was, and in that flash of alarm he was back on the roof, gasping, convinced he was about to die. The very state of being unable to relax made him more reactive to the world around him, and more vulnerable to the next trigger.

His work as a roofer ended early because he could no longer tolerate being on a roof in the open air—it felt too exposed, too close to the memory. Now he stays mostly inside, and his wife runs most errands. Their marriage has grown strained; she feels he pushes her away, and he knows he does, but he cannot stop flinching.

What finally brought Karim to seek help was the news that his daughter is expecting a baby. He desperately wants to be part of his grandchild’s life, but he is terrified of the panic that will come whenever he hears that child cry or play. Worse, he is secretly afraid that something from the toxic exposure lingers in him and might somehow harm the baby. He lies awake at night, his wife breathing beside him, wondering if he will ever feel safe enough to hold his grandchild.
